name: Ethical Purchasing Group - SIA Project 22 23
description:
The system supports the management of an Ethical Purchasing Group (EPS),
    known in Italian as a Gruppo di Acquisto Solidale (GAS), associated with a
    km-zero fruit and vegetable store. The purpose of the system is to connect
    groups of customers with local farmers and store employees, supporting a
    conscious purchasing process based on knowledge of product origin, quality,
    characteristics, availability, and price.

    The operating cycle of the purchasing group is organized on a weekly basis.
    Farmers provide estimates of the products they can supply between Friday
    at noon and Saturday morning. For each available product, farmers specify
    the product type, quantity, price, and optionally additional crop
    characteristics such as size, quality, or ripeness.

    The information system maintains a catalogue of products containing
    descriptions, photographs, the unit of measurement used for sale, and the
    minimum and maximum quantities that can be ordered. Each availability
    entered by a farmer refers to one of the products contained in the catalogue.

    Customers can browse the offers provided by the different farmers and place
    orders by selecting products and specifying the desired quantities. Customers
    are representatives of purchasing groups, such as families or groups of
    people, and only the registered representative of each group can submit an
    order.

    Orders can be entered directly by customers through the web system or by
    store employees on behalf of customers. Before an order can be confirmed,
    the system checks that the quantities selected respect the minimum order
    constraints defined for each product. If the minimum quantities are not met,
    the customer must modify the order. After completion, the system sends an
    order summary to the customer by email.

    Customer orders initially remain in an entered state until farmers confirm
    the actual quantities available by Monday morning. If the available
    quantities are sufficient to satisfy all orders, the orders are confirmed.
    When the available quantity of a product is insufficient, the system applies
    precedence rules based on customer priority and removes unavailable
    quantities from lower-priority orders.

    Orders modified because of limited product availability are placed in a
    modified state and must be reviewed and explicitly accepted by customers.
    If every product in an order becomes unavailable, the order is cancelled.

    After farmers confirm product availability, the system automatically
    performs payment for the quantities actually included in the order.
    Payments are made through a personal virtual wallet associated with each
    customer. Customers can recharge their wallet through the store at any time.

    If a customer's wallet balance is insufficient immediately after order
    placement, the customer receives an email warning, but the order remains
    valid. If the balance is insufficient when the automatic payment is executed,
    the customer receives an SMS and has until Monday evening to recharge the
    wallet. If the required balance is still unavailable at that time, the order
    is cancelled.

    Once payment has been successfully completed, customers can reserve a time
    slot for collecting their products from the store. Store employees can view
    the pickup schedule at the beginning of their shifts and prepare the packages
    corresponding to customer orders. When a customer arrives, the employee
    confirms the collection of the order.

    If a customer fails to collect the order at the scheduled time, the system
    sends an SMS reminder. If the order has not been collected by Friday, the
    order is marked as forfeited and the customer's fair-play score is updated.

    Farmers deliver their products to the store by Tuesday evening. Store
    employees confirm the receipt of the delivered quantities. If the goods
    have not arrived by 4 p.m. on Tuesday, the system sends an SMS reminder.
    If the goods have still not been delivered by 8 p.m., the related customer
    orders are updated, the missing amount is credited back to the affected
    customers with an additional 20 percent bonus, and the customers are
    informed of the delivery problem.

    The system maintains a fair-play score for each customer. The score represents
    the reliability of the customer with respect to previous orders and is used
    as a precedence criterion when product availability is insufficient.
    The score is computed from the number of completed orders, reminders received,
    forfeited pickups, and modified orders. Customers with higher fair-play scores
    are given precedence over customers with lower scores when limited quantities
    must be allocated among competing orders.

highLevelGoals: Farmers aim to efficiently submit estimates of available products, including type, quantity, price, and characteristics, to the system.
Farmers seek to confirm the final quantities of products they can supply to ensure accurate order processing and fulfillment.
Farmers aim to deliver their products to the store within the specified timeframe to facilitate subsequent customer pickups.
Customers aim to easily browse available products from local farmers, understand their characteristics, and place orders for desired quantities.
Customers seek to have their orders processed correctly, receive notifications about any modifications due to availability, and confirm final order details.
Customers aim to maintain a sufficient balance in their virtual wallet for automatic payments and be informed of any payment-related issues.
Customers desire the ability to schedule a pickup time and confirm the collection of their orders from the store.
Customers aim to uphold a positive fair-play score to ensure priority in order allocation and demonstrate their reliability within the purchasing group.
Store employees aim to assist customers with order placement, modifications, and ensure all order details are accurately managed within the system.
Store employees seek to manage customer virtual wallet recharges and resolve payment issues to ensure smooth and successful transactions.
Store employees aim to efficiently manage the pickup schedule, prepare customer orders, and confirm successful collection of goods.
Store employees aim to confirm the receipt of products from farmers, track delivery status, and manage any discrepancies or delays.
lowLevelGoals: Farmer can submit an estimate of available products, including type, estimated quantity, price per unit, and specific characteristics, to the system.
Farmer can update an existing product estimate with revised estimated quantity, price per unit, or characteristics.
Farmer can retrieve and review a list of all their currently submitted product estimates.
Farmer can confirm the final actual quantity for a specific product estimate they can supply.
Farmer can view a list of all products for which they have confirmed actual quantities.
Farmer can report a discrepancy between the confirmed quantity and the actual quantity available for delivery.
Farmer can mark a specific product delivery as dispatched from their farm.
Farmer can view the scheduled delivery times for their products to the store.
Farmer can report an anticipated delay in product delivery and provide an updated estimated arrival time.
Customer can browse a list of available products, optionally filtering by product type, farmer, or price range.
Customer can view detailed information for a specific product, including its characteristics, origin, and farmer information.
Customer can add a specified quantity of a product to their shopping cart.
Customer can place an order for all items currently in their shopping cart.
Customer can view the current details of their active orders, including items, quantities, and total price.
Customer can receive a notification if their order has been modified due to product availability or other reasons.
Customer can confirm the final details of their order after any modifications have been applied.
Customer can cancel an order before it reaches a certain processing stage.
Customer can view their current virtual wallet balance.
Customer can initiate a recharge of their virtual wallet using a specified payment method and amount.
Customer can receive an alert when their virtual wallet balance falls below a predefined threshold.
Customer can view a history of all transactions made from and to their virtual wallet.
Customer can select and schedule a preferred pickup time for their order from available time slots.
Customer can view the details of their scheduled order pickup, including time and location.
Customer can confirm the successful collection of their order from the store.
Customer can receive a reminder notification for an upcoming order pickup.
Customer can view their current fair-play score.
Customer can receive a notification when their fair-play score is updated (e.g., after an order cancellation or successful pickup).
Customer can access information explaining how the fair-play score is calculated and its implications.
Store Employee can search for customer orders using criteria such as customer ID, order ID, or order status.
Store Employee can assist a customer by adding items to their cart and initiating an order on their behalf.
Store Employee can modify an existing customer order, such as adjusting quantities or removing items, on behalf of the customer.
Store Employee can view the complete order history for a specific customer.
Store Employee can process a recharge for a customer's virtual wallet, specifying the amount and payment method.
Store Employee can view the virtual wallet balance for a specific customer.
Store Employee can manually resolve a payment issue for a customer, such as marking an order as paid or adjusting a balance.
Store Employee can generate a report detailing payment transactions for a specified period or customer.
Store Employee can view the schedule of all customer order pickups for the current day.
Store Employee can mark a specific customer order as prepared and ready for pickup.
Store Employee can confirm that a customer has successfully collected their order.
Store Employee can reschedule a customer's pickup time for an order if requested or necessary.
Store Employee can view a list of all expected incoming product deliveries from farmers.
Store Employee can confirm the receipt of a farmer's delivery, including recording actual quantities received.
Store Employee can report any discrepancies found in a farmer's delivery, such as quantity mismatches or damaged goods.
Store Employee can update the status of a farmer's delivery (e.g., 'received', 'partially received', 'delayed').

baselineCritiques.actors: The identified actors (Farmer, Customer, Store Employee) are correct and cover all the active entities described in the system. However, the description mentions that "Customers are representatives of purchasing groups, such as families or groups of people." While the system interacts with the representative, the "Purchasing Group" (or GAS) is a distinct entity in the domain that holds the collective order and fair-play score context. In GORE, it is often beneficial to explicitly identify the "Purchasing Group Representative" or acknowledge the group as a stakeholder/actor context to distinguish from individual customers in other systems. More importantly, the description states that "Store employees can enter orders... on behalf of customers." This confirms the Store Employee role. The main potential omission is the explicit distinction of the "Purchasing Group" as an actor or the specific role of the "Group Representative" if the system treats the group as a first-class citizen for data (e.g., group-level fair play or orders). Given the description says "only the registered representative of each group can submit an order," the actor is effectively the Representative. The current label "Customer" is acceptable but slightly generic. A more precise label might be "Group Representative" or "Customer Representative". However, "Customer" is not incorrect. The score is high because the core actors are present and correctly described.

evaluation.rationale:
The three Low-Level Goals (LLGs) are all directly relevant to the parent High-Level Goal (HLG) 'Provide product availability and details'. 

1. **llg_001 (Submit product estimate)**: Directly supports the core action of providing availability. It aligns with the requirement that farmers specify product type, quantity, price, and characteristics.
2. **llg_002 (Update product estimate)**: Supports the 'efficiently submit' aspect by allowing corrections or adjustments before the final confirmation window closes. This is a standard and necessary capability for data entry workflows.
3. **llg_003 (View submitted product estimates)**: Supports the 'efficiently' aspect by allowing the farmer to verify what has been submitted. This is a reasonable and non-duplicative capability for user control and error checking.

None of the LLGs are duplicated, contradictory, or unrelated. They represent a coherent set of CRUD-like operations (Create, Update, Read) necessary for the farmer to manage their availability submissions. There are no missing essential capabilities for this specific HLG scope (e.g., deleting an estimate might be considered, but 'Update' often covers correction, and 'View' covers verification; deletion is not explicitly required by the text for the *submission* phase, though it might be implied for re-submission, it is not an *essential* missing capability that invalidates the current set). missing_hlg_evaluation.rationale: The project description outlines a weekly purchasing cycle involving farmers, customers, and store employees. The current High-Level Goals (HLGs) comprehensively cover the functional intentions of all identified actors: Farmers (providing availability, confirming quantities, delivering goods), Customers (browsing/ordering, managing order status/accuracy, handling payments/wallets, scheduling/collecting pickups, maintaining fair-play scores), and Store Employees (supporting orders, managing payments, coordinating pickups, verifying deliveries). Specific workflow steps such as email/SMS notifications, precedence rules based on fair-play scores, and delivery delay handling are operational details or sub-goals already covered by the broader stakeholder intentions defined in the existing HLGs (e.g., 'Ensure order accuracy and fulfillment', 'Manage personal payment for purchases', 'Verify farmer deliveries'). There are no distinct, documented functional intentions for any actor that are absent from the current list.

branch_002.rationale: The original High-Level Goal 'Confirm actual product quantities' is supported by the project description, which states that farmers confirm actual quantities available by Monday morning. However, the bottom-up reconstruction 'Manage Farmer's Product Supply Commitments' is broader and potentially overlaps with the existing HLG 'Provide product availability and details'. The specific action of confirming final quantities is a distinct step in the workflow (occurring after initial estimates and before order confirmation) that ensures accurate order processing. The original goal is reasonably scoped and distinct from 'Provide product availability and details' (which refers to the initial estimation phase between Friday and Saturday). Therefore, the original goal should be kept as it accurately reflects a specific, supported functional intention of the Farmer actor. The parent HLG 'Confirm actual product quantities' requires the farmer to finalize the supply commitment. The current LLGs cover the core action (llg_001: Confirm actual product quantity) and a reasonable verification step (llg_002: View confirmed product quantities). The third LLG (llg_003: Report quantity discrepancy) is not explicitly required by the parent HLG's description ('confirm the final quantities... to ensure accurate order processing'). While the documentation mentions that store employees confirm receipt and handle discrepancies later in the cycle (Tuesday), the farmer's specific role in the 'Confirm' phase is to provide the final numbers. Reporting a discrepancy *after* confirmation is not a distinct capability explicitly mandated by the parent HLG's wording, which focuses on the act of confirming the quantities themselves. Furthermore, llg_003 is not contradicted by the documentation, but rather represents an optional or subsequent workflow step that is not essential to the definition of 'Confirming actual product quantities' in this context. Since no essential capability explicitly required by the parent is missing, and no LLG is contradicted by the documentation, the decomposition is acceptable.

replacement_request.rationale: The original HLG 'Conveniently collect purchased goods' is too broad and mixes scheduling with the physical act of collection. The project description explicitly details a workflow where customers reserve a time slot, employees prepare packages, and employees confirm collection. The focus should be narrowed to the specific functional intention of managing the pickup process, which includes reserving the slot and the subsequent confirmation by the store, as this is the distinct operational phase after payment. The actor remains the Customer, who initiates the reservation and is the subject of the collection.
replacement_request.generation_project_description: The system supports the management of an Ethical Purchasing Group (EPS) associated with a km-zero fruit and vegetable store. After payment is successfully completed for a customer's order, the customer can reserve a specific time slot for collecting their products from the store. Store employees can view the pickup schedule at the beginning of their shifts to prepare the packages corresponding to customer orders. When a customer arrives at the store, the employee confirms the collection of the order. If a customer fails to collect the order at the scheduled time, the system sends an SMS reminder. If the order has not been collected by Friday, the order is marked as forfeited and the customer's fair-play score is updated.

missing_hlg_evaluation.rationale: The project description outlines a weekly purchasing cycle involving farmers, customers, and store employees. The current High-Level Goals (HLGs) comprehensively cover the functional intentions of all identified actors: Farmers (providing availability, confirming quantities, delivering goods), Customers (browsing/ordering, managing payments/wallets, collecting goods, maintaining fair-play scores), and Store Employees (managing orders, overseeing payments, coordinating pickups, verifying deliveries). Specific workflow steps such as order modification due to availability, automatic payment execution, SMS/email notifications, and fair-play score calculation are operational details or narrower variants of the existing broad stakeholder intentions (e.g., 'Manage personal payment for purchases' covers the wallet and notification logic; 'Maintain a reliable purchasing record' covers the fair-play score usage). There are no distinct, documented functional intentions for any actor that are absent from the current HLG list.

branch_005.rationale: The low-level goals collectively describe the complete process a customer undertakes to select products, manage their selection in a temporary order (often called a shopping cart), and then submit that selection as a final order. This entire sequence is aimed at allowing customers to successfully place an order for available products.

branch_005.rationale: The original High-Level Goal 'Enable customers to browse products and place orders' is semantically identical to the existing High-Level Goal 'Discover and order local produce' (which describes the same intention: browsing offers and placing orders). The bottom-up reconstruction 'Enable Customers to Place Orders' also confirms this single functional intention. According to the guidelines, one should not keep several HLGs that merely split one stakeholder intention into wording variants or duplicate existing goals. Since 'Discover and order local produce' already covers this specific functional intention for the Customer actor, the original goal is redundant and should be removed to avoid duplication.

branch_007.rationale: The original High-Level Goal 'Enable customers to schedule product collection' is supported by the project description, which states that 'customers can reserve a time slot for collecting their products'. However, the bottom-up reconstruction 'Enable customers to manage their product collection time slots' is more faithful to the full scope of the low-level goals, which include not just scheduling (booking) but also viewing, cancelling, and modifying bookings. replacement_request.rationale: The original goal 'Enable customers to schedule product collection' is too narrow. The project description explicitly states that customers can 'reserve a time slot', but the broader context of managing the pickup process implies the ability to view, cancel, or modify these slots as part of the overall order management lifecycle. The evaluator's instruction specifically requests updating the goal to reflect the 'management of collection time slots (including booking, viewing, cancelling, and modifying)'. Therefore, the goal name and description must be broadened to encompass these management actions rather than just the initial scheduling/reservation.
replacement_request.generation_project_description: The system supports the management of an Ethical Purchasing Group (EPS) associated with a km-zero fruit and vegetable store. Once payment for an order has been successfully completed, customers can manage their product collection time slots. This includes booking a specific time slot for collecting products, viewing existing reservations, cancelling a reservation, and modifying a previously booked time slot. Store employees can view the pickup schedule to prepare packages. The system ensures that customers can effectively manage their collection logistics after payment.

missing_hlg_evaluation.rationale: The project description outlines a weekly purchasing cycle involving farmers, customers, and store employees. The current High-Level Goals (HLGs) comprehensively cover the functional intentions of all identified actors: Farmers (providing availability, confirming quantities, delivering goods), Customers (browsing/ordering, managing payments/wallets, scheduling pickups, maintaining fair-play scores), and Store Employees (managing orders, handling payments, coordinating pickups, verifying deliveries). Specific workflow steps such as order modification due to availability, automatic payment execution, SMS/email notifications, and fair-play score calculation are operational details or narrower variants of the existing broad stakeholder intentions (e.g., 'Manage personal payment for purchases' covers the wallet and payment logic; 'Maintain a reliable purchasing record' covers the fair-play score). There are no distinct, documented functional intentions for any actor that are absent from the current HLG list.

branch_005.rationale: These low-level goals collectively describe the complete process a customer undertakes to select products, build an order, and then submit that order. They cover product discovery, order item management (add, modify, remove), and final order submission, all essential steps in a customer's purchasing journey.

branch_005.rationale: The original High-Level Goal 'Enable customers to browse products and place orders' is semantically identical to the existing High-Level Goal 'Discover and order local produce' (which describes the same intention: browsing offers and placing orders). Therefore, the original goal should be removed to avoid duplication.

branch_007.rationale: The project description explicitly states that 'Once payment has been successfully completed, customers can reserve a time slot for collecting their products from the store.' It also mentions that if a customer fails to collect at the scheduled time, reminders are sent, implying the existence of a schedule that can be viewed or managed. The original High-Level Goal 'Enable customers to manage product collection time slots' accurately captures this functional intention. The bottom-up reconstruction 'Manage Customer Product Collection Time Slots' aligns with this. There is no other High-Level Goal for the Customer actor that covers this specific aspect of pickup logistics (other Customer HLGs cover ordering, payment, and fair-play scores). The scope is appropriate and supported by the documentation. The parent High-Level Goal (HLG) explicitly requires customers to be able to 'book, view, cancel, and modify' their reserved time slots. The current Low-Level Goals (LLGs) cover all four of these capabilities: llg_001 (reserve/book), llg_002 (retrieve/view), llg_003 (cancel), and llg_004 (modify). The documentation supports these actions as part of the customer's post-payment workflow. There are no contradictions with the documentation, and no essential capabilities explicitly required by the parent HLG are missing. The sibling HLGs regarding store employee logistics do not conflict with these customer-facing management goals.
